questions.question: For a linear objective $z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2$ with $c_1,c_2$ not both zero, which set of points $(x_1,x_2)$ is the objective line for the value $\bar z$?
options: All points where $z$ is as large as possible

questions.question: For a fixed objective $z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2$ with $c_2\ne0$, what happens to the objective line $z=\bar z$ when the value $\bar z$ is changed?
options: It turns about the origin, its slope changing with $\bar z$
It shifts parallel to itself and keeps its slope $-c_1/c_2$
It stays put; only the label $\bar z$ attached to it changes
It shifts and also steepens, as $\bar z$ enters its equation

questions.question: For an objective $z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2$ with $c_2=0$ and $c_1\ne0$, what do the objective lines look like in the $(x_1,x_2)$-plane?
Where does the objective line $3x_1+2x_2=12$, the line $z=12$ of $z=3x_1+2x_2$, meet the $x_1$-axis and the $x_2$-axis?
With $x_1$ on the horizontal and $x_2$ on the vertical axis, what is the slope of each objective line of $z=4x_1+5x_2$?
Which equation describes the objective line of $z=x_1+2x_2$ that passes through the point $(2,3)$?
Which displacement $(\Delta x_1,\Delta x_2)$ of a plan raises the value of $z=3x_1-2x_2$?
For an objective $z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2$ with $c_2<0$, how does the objective line $z=\bar z$ move as $\bar z$ increases?
options: Up, since a higher value always means a higher line
Down, since its intercept $\bar z/c_2$ decreases
It turns, since its slope depends on the value $\bar z$
Down, but only when $c_1<0$ holds as well

questions.question: For the objective $z=3x_1+2x_2$, why can the objective lines $z=6$ and $z=12$ have no point in common?
options: They share their slope and also their intercept
They do meet, as any two lines in a plane meet
A common point would need both $z=6$ and $z=12$
They cannot be disjoint: equal slopes make them one line

questions.question: Starting from $z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2$ with $c_1=3$ and $c_2=2$, which change alters the slope of the objective lines $z=\bar z$?
Which slope-intercept form describes the objective line $z=6$ of the objective $z=2x_1-3x_2$?
The point $(2,5)$ gives $z=26$ for $z=3x_1+4x_2$. Which other point lies on the same objective line?
For the objective $z=5x_2$, that is $c_1=0$ and $c_2=5$, which equation describes the objective line $z=10$?
Why does the definition of an objective line for $z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2$ require at least one of $c_1,c_2$ to be nonzero?
options: If $c_1=c_2=0$, $z=\bar z$ holds everywhere or nowhere
So that the slope $-c_1/c_2$ is always defined
So that the line $z=\bar z$ lies in the first quadrant
So that a larger $\bar z$ always moves the line upwards

questions.question: How are the objective lines of $z=x_1+2x_2$ related to those of $w=2x_1+4x_2$?
options: Parallel, but no line of one is a line of the other
They are the same lines, each one carrying $w=2z$
The lines of $w$ are twice as steep as those of $z$
Different, because the two objectives differ

questions.question: For an objective $z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2$, the objective line $z=6$ is $x_2=-2x_1+3$ and the objective line $z=12$ is $x_2=-2x_1+6$. What are $c_1$ and $c_2$?
The objective lines of $z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2$ have slope 2, and moving a plan straight up, raising $x_2$ with $x_1$ fixed, increases $z$. What are the signs of $c_1$ and $c_2$?
